name: Light Cadmium
lede: Light Cadmium is a warm, slightly dull gold, named after cadmium yellow light, the pale end of the cadmium sulfide pigments.

sections.title: The pigment
sections.body: Cadmium yellow is a sulfide of the metal cadmium, and Ball credits the chemist Stromeyer with early work on it [1]. Altering how the compound is made gives orange instead of yellow, since the hue depends on the grain size [1]. Ball says it was a rich, opaque yellow that does not fade in sunlight, but the supply from zinc smelting was too small for it to matter until the 1840s [1]. Some oil painting in France and Germany used it from about 1829 [1]. Jarman instead gives the start of modern production as the First World War, so the books disagree on the early history [1][2].

sections.title: Light, in the tube
sections.body:
In a modern paint chart, *cadmium yellow light* is the pigment PY 35 [3]. Gurney uses it as a pigment that comes close to a yellow primary for subtractive mixing [3]. The Pigment Compendium records that early light cadmium sulfide pigments contained up to 30 per cent cadmium oxalate, which made them unstable, fading in air and light [4].

The swatch here is duller than the paint: the ISCC-NBS block is dark yellow, 3.1 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale, and our library traces the name to Ridgway's plate IV of 1912 [5]. Compare [[cadmium-lemon]], the paler member of the family [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color this close appears in 523 works, or 2.2 per cent [6]. It peaks in the 1400s, at 3.4 per cent of 945 paintings, which is long before cadmium existed, so the match is gold or ochre, not the pigment [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings [6].
